passage:
Day one, Tuesday. The course sold to students in ones and twos, and the sales chart was flat. "We keep asking why students won't pay," Divyansh said, tapping the marker on the desk. "Wrong question. Who is better off when a student learns this?" Shalini leaned in and started a list: exam-coaching centres, schools, parents' groups.
Day four. Divyansh phoned a coaching centre owner and asked about the centre's weakest subject. It happened to be the topic the team's videos already covered.
Day seventeen. The centre bought 150 seats for its batch. The videos did not change at all; only the person the team talked to did.

qa.q: How many seats did the coaching centre buy?
What was Shalini feeling when Divyansh asked the new question?
qa.a: Shalini was curious and hopeful: leaning in and starting a list right away shows the question opened something up.

qa.q: What other approach could the team use to check that the new customer is right, and why?
qa.a: They could use time-boxing: set a few weeks and a target number of centres, so a weak result shows quickly instead of dragging on.

qa.q: How might the centre's owner see the offer?
qa.a: The owner sees a fix for the centre's weakest subject that many students can use, which is a different pitch from asking each student to pay.

grounding: The passage shows a team asking who benefits from students learning and taking the same course to a new kind of buyer.

passage:
Tushar sir leaned against the whiteboard when Santosh complained that no student would pay for the exam-prep videos. "Santosh, I've been exactly where you are. At twenty-five I had two hundred maths videos and maybe fifteen paying students. Every week we asked the same question: why won't students pay?
Then one night my co-founder asked a different one: who actually gains when a student learns this? Parents, yes. But also coaching institutes. Their name goes up on the results board. They need good material, and they buy in bulk.
Same videos. Different buyer. The next month we sat in the office of a coaching centre in Kota. They bought licences for four hundred students in one go.
So stop asking why students don't pay. Ask who wins when they learn."

qa.q: How many students did the Kota coaching centre buy licences for?
qa.a: Four hundred students, in one go.

qa.q: How might young Tushar have felt when the co-founder asked the different question?
qa.a: He was probably surprised and excited, seeing a way out of weeks of frustration.

qa.q: Which choice in the story turned things around, and why?
qa.a: Changing the question from why students won't pay to who gains when they learn, because it revealed coaching institutes as bulk buyers.

qa.q: How do the coaching institutes see the videos?
qa.a: For institutes, good material improves results that carry their name, so the videos are worth buying in bulk.

grounding: It shows a young founder's team asking who benefits from students learning instead of why students won't pay, and selling the same content to coaching institutes in bulk.

passage:
Disha and Kalyani had three weeks of money left and a spoken-English course nobody bought. College students downloaded the free lessons, loved them and never paid.
On the bus back from yet another campus stall, stuck in traffic on the ring road, Kalyani said, "We keep asking why students won't pay. What if they're not the ones who should?"
Disha frowned. "Then who?"
"Who benefits when a student speaks English well? Parents. Colleges, for placement numbers. And the coaching institutes that prepare kids for interviews. They have hundreds of students and a budget."
By the time the bus reached their stop, they had a list of twelve institutes. With the clock ticking, they didn't rebuild anything. They printed the same course outline with a bulk price and spent the next nine days visiting. Three institutes signed, for over six hundred students between them.

qa.a: Three, for over six hundred students between them.

qa.q: Why did Disha frown at Kalyani's question?
qa.a: Disha was puzzled and a bit doubtful, having only ever thought of students as the buyers.

qa.q: Why was not rebuilding the course a smart move?
qa.a: With three weeks of money left, reusing the same course with a bulk price let them test the new buyers quickly.

qa.q: How might the coaching institutes see the course?
qa.a: They get ready material for hundreds of students preparing for interviews, which helps them deliver what they promise.

grounding: It shows founders reframing their customer from students to the coaching institutes that benefit from students learning, and selling the same course to them in bulk.
